description:
We’re a Malaysia-based team passionate about AI, software engineering, cybersecurity, and building solutions to real-world challenges.

For NASA Space Apps 2026, we’re exploring how satellite data and intelligent technologies can help people better understand changes happening on Earth.

We enjoy combining technical innovation with practical impact and welcome collaborators with interests in GIS, remote sensing, data science, or product design.
summary: Hearthbeat is an Earth Information Jukebox: a free web app that turns NASA's daily Earth data into music, so anyone can hear how home is doing. NASA's Earth Information Center shows rain, air quality and a warming climate as colour maps, which leaves out the 2.2 billion people living with a vision impairment, and astronauts who can see home from orbit but cannot hear it. Hearthbeat pairs each EIC frame with sound generated live in the browser: rain becomes raindrops, PM2.5 above the WHO guideline becomes a heartbeat, warming since 1880 becomes a rising melody, and night lights and lightning seen from the ISS join as bells and marimba. Choose any place and ask three plain questions, play a one-minute Home song, explore five tracks on a 3D globe, or open Together, where an astronaut and their family hear each other's side of the planet. Eyes-closed mode, speech, keyboard control and vibration make every part usable without sight. The data is refreshed and checked every day, and the site is published only when all 190 automated tests pass.
details:
Links

  • Live app: https://yantongggg.github.io/Hearbeat_NASA/
  • Source code: https://github.com/yantongggg/Hearbeat_NASA
  • Project document (PDF, with team poster): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1zuFNzkKbi5xnspaUoGEWK4dDXWwrbmNW/view
  • Project video (4:28) and all materials: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/19wLiQuMWGdlQFvEEmqjHYQK5JBhnh27x

What it does Hearthbeat turns five NASA data sets into five musical voices:

  • Rain (EIC / SVS 5149, GEOS-FP): raindrops, from 1 a second in light rain to 10 a second at 20 mm/h.
  • Air quality (GEOS-CF v2 PM2.5; EIC / SVS 5151): above the WHO 24-hour guideline of 15 µg/m³, a heartbeat from 60 to 140 beats a minute; below it, a calm bass.
  • Warming (GISTEMP v4, 1880–2025): a melody on the D major pentatonic scale, from D4 at −1 °C to A5 at +2 °C.
  • Night lights (SVS 5313, Black Marble, 2012–2023): bells.
  • Lightning seen from the ISS (SVS 5011, LIS on the ISS, 2017–2023): marimba taps, 1 to 6 a second.

Four ways in:

  • Hear my home: choose any place and ask "Is it raining?", "Is the air clean?", "How much warmer than in 1951–1980?". Each answer is a short sound, then NASA's number.
  • Home song: all five voices as one song for one place, in D major at 84 beats a minute, about a minute long.
  • Explore: five jukebox tracks over a 3D globe. Move the listening point by click, tap or arrow keys; a timeline steps through the last five days, or 146 years of warming.
  • Together: the astronaut sees the globe through a porthole that follows the ISS on NASA's predicted trajectory and hears home; the family sees where their astronaut is and hears the Earth passing below the station.

Check-ups for class pose four questions answered by ear, with a CSV log for listening tests, and a classroom pack in English and Chinese.

How it works A Python pipeline runs every day on GitHub Actions. It downloads NASA's newest EIC frames, reads every pixel back to a value through NASA's own colour scale, and checks value ranges, missing data, dates and map alignment before anything replaces the published data. PM2.5 numbers come straight from GEOS-CF over OPeNDAP, because reading them from the picture gave values about four times too low. A failing layer keeps its last good data or is switched off with a reason; nothing is simulated. In the browser, TypeScript, three.js and the Web Audio API read the value under the listening point and synthesize the sound live, so the EIC frame on screen, the spoken value and the sound always come from the same place and the same data step.

Validation

  • Values read from NASA pictures were compared with NASA's raw model output for the same hour and place. Temperature correlation is 0.998–0.999. Rain correlation is 0.33–0.82, so rain amounts are presented as a guide.
  • 190 automated tests run before every deploy: 75 data pipeline, 51 unit and 64 in-browser, including axe accessibility scans (WCAG 2.1 A/AA) and keyboard-only use.
  • Sound levels were measured, so the music stays calm and never clips.

What the data tells you by ear

  • Kuala Lumpur's melody climbs after the 1970s as the city warms by +1.03 °C (2020s vs 1951–1980).
  • On 14 November 2026, Kuala Lumpur's air (75 µg/m³) beat at 116 a minute while Kuching's (10 µg/m³) was a calm bass.
  • Kuala Lumpur has lightning all year; Florida's comes only in summer.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Blind and low-vision learners can explore NASA data on their own. Malaysia's National Eye Survey estimated 1.2% blindness and 5.9% moderate visual impairment among adults aged 50 and over.
  • Classrooms and museums get a free tool and a classroom pack.
  • Families apart, and crews on long missions, share a sound of home made from data.
  • Everyone hears air quality and climate change as something felt, not only read.

It is free, needs no install or account, and runs on any phone or laptop with headphones; running costs are close to zero. It relates to SDGs 3, 4, 10, 11 and 13.

Tools and languages

  • Pipeline: Python with NumPy, Pillow, Requests, netCDF4 and FFmpeg.
  • App: TypeScript with three.js, d3-geo, Web Audio API and Web Speech API.
  • Tests: Vite, Vitest, Playwright and axe-core.
  • Hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

What makes it creative Existing sonifications are pre-rendered pieces and existing maps are visual only. Hearthbeat is live, daily and place-based: any place on Earth, today's NASA data, heard as warm music in one key, with the exact number always one step away. Together turns the same data into a shared experience for an astronaut and their family.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: we measured it, and every limit is stated in the app.
  • Accessibility first: eyes-closed mode, screen-reader text, keyboard, speech and vibration.
  • Calm sound: major keys, no alarms, and the air shown as a guide, not a health warning.
  • Rules: only public-domain third-party audio with no voices, and no images or voices of anyone under 18.
  • Limits: no blind or low-vision listener has tested Hearthbeat yet, and it has not been tested with screen readers or on a real phone. Our next step is a listening test with blind and low-vision students in Malaysia.

Team D3stiny: Chye Yan Tong, Hong Rui Yi (NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Kuala Lumpur). Hearthbeat is an independent open-source project (Apache 2.0); it uses NASA's open data but is not a NASA product and is not endorsed by NASA.
